newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to keep troops in riot-torn province.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to keep troops in riot-torn province.

text.p: Indonesia will maintain the 3,000 troops it deployed in West Kalimantan even though peace has gradually returned to riot-torn province, Antara news agency reported on Sunday.
The official agency quoted Tanjungpura Military Commander Major-General Namuri Anoem as saying on Saturday that the armed forces had no intention of withdrawing the soldiers yet.
"Even though the overall situation in many regencies is under control, we still hope that the ethnic riots could be immediately settled," he said in provincial capital Pontianak.
Antara gave no other details. The Tanjungpura Military Command oversees Kalimantan's four provinces on the Indonesian side of Borneo island.

Ethnic riots started in the province bordering Malaysia's Sarawak state in late December in what police said was a fight between Dayak and Maduran youths over a girl at a concert in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak.
The fighting between ethnic Dayaks and Madurans, who are migrants from Madura island off the main island of Java, spread to other parts of the province.
In Sanggau, 140 km (90 miles) east of Pontianak, Maduran families have taken refuge in army camps after a series of fights between the two groups.

Anoem said the clash was the fifth such ethnic riot to hit West Kalimantan since 1977, and had killed at least 49 people. He said 12 people had been killed in Sanggau Ledo alone, but gave no details about fatalities in Sanggau.
Anoem also said the military pledged to take stern action against rioters.
Residents in Pontianak told Reuters on Sunday the capital was calm and that soldiers were still on patrol there.
Antara quoted West Kalimantan Police Chief Colonel Erwin Achman as saying 68 people had been arrested after the riots. He said 13 of the detainees would be tried on charges of inciting the riots.
A military official said in Pontianak on Saturday traditional ceremonies to ease tension had been held in several places in the interior between the two groups.
Most Dayaks are Christians while the Maduran migrants, like most Indonesians, are Moslems. At least 19 people have died in religious and ethnic riots in Indonesia since October.
